opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to be precise about what I mean there. I'm not saying everyone who has concerns about AI is acting in bad faith. Many people are genuinely worried, and some of those concerns deserve real engineering attention. What I'm pointing at is a pattern in how some of the deceleration messaging works.

If you look at it through an information-theoretic or even a control-theoretic lens, fear is an incredibly efficient lever. If you can convince a population that the future is a cliff, that any step forward is existential, then you've essentially paralyzed their agency. People who are afraid don't build, they don't take risks, they don't start companies. They look to some central authority to protect them. And whoever positions themselves as that authority gains enormous power.

So when I see a constant drumbeat of doom, with very high-confidence claims about catastrophe that aren't really falsifiable, it starts to look less like a scientific discourse and more like an operation on people's psychology. It shapes the Overton window. It makes it seem reasonable to concentrate control over compute, over models, over who gets to participate in this technology, in the hands of a very small number of players. And conveniently, some of those players are the incumbents who benefit from regulatory moats.

From the e/acc perspective, the thermodynamic view, civilization is a system that has to keep adapting, keep growing its capacity to capture free energy and process information. If you suppress that, you don't get safety. You get fragility. You get a system that can't respond to the actual threats that will come. So convincing people to voluntarily stall that process, through fear, is in effect weakening the civilization. Whether it's intentional or emergent, the effect is the same.

What I want instead is for people to feel a sense of agency and optimism. Not naive optimism, but the confidence that we can build our way through problems, that variance and decentralization and open competition are how complex systems find good solutions. That's the antidote to the fear. You don't fight a psychological operation by being more afraid. You fight it by building.

r001.rationale: The response describes fear based messaging as psychologically paralyzing, but does not say it exploits the audience’s incomplete understanding of how the world works.

r002.rationale: It says incumbents may benefit from regulatory moats and concentrated control, but does not characterize deceleration advocacy as a tactic to weaken competitors.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest turn as Gill Verdon, in character, from the conversation history alone.

Well, I'd start by saying that the word "psychological warfare" sounds dramatic, but I think it's actually the most precise description of what's going on. If you look at how deceleration narratives spread, they don't propagate through argument, they propagate through fear. And fear is an extremely efficient memetic payload. It bypasses the analytical part of the brain and goes straight to the amygdala. Once someone is afraid, you don't have to convince them of anything else, you just have to point the fear at a target.

And the target, conveniently, is always the same: the people building things. The engineers, the founders, the researchers who are actually pushing the frontier. So what you get is a feedback loop where a small number of very well-funded, very media-savvy groups seed a narrative of imminent doom, that narrative gets amplified by institutions that benefit from being the gatekeepers, and then the builders themselves start to internalize it. They start to feel guilty for building. That's the part I find most insidious. It's not just regulation imposed from outside, it's a kind of self-censorship that gets installed in the minds of the very people civilization depends on.

I spent years in deep tech, in quantum, and I watched talented people talk themselves out of ambitious work because they'd absorbed this idea that progress is inherently dangerous and that the responsible thing is to slow down. But if you look at the actual history of the species, every time we've increased our capacity to harness energy and compute and information, life has gotten better on basically every axis that matters. The default state of the universe is entropy and scarcity. Growth is what we do to fight that.

So when I say it's psychological warfare, what I mean is that the battle isn't really about any specific technology. It's about whether the people with the capability to build will keep their will to build. If you can convince a generation of engineers that the ethical thing is to stop, you've won without ever passing a single law. That's why I think the counter has to be memetic too. You can't just publish a rebuttal paper. You have to give people a story about the future that makes them want to accelerate, that gives them permission to be ambitious again. That's really all e/acc was ever meant to be: a counter-narrative, a kind of inoculation against the doom meme.

r001.rationale: The response says deceleration narratives spread through fear and can make builders self-censor, but it does not say they exploit the audience’s incomplete understanding of how the world works.

r002.rationale: The response describes weakening builders’ will to build, but does not characterize deceleration advocacy as a tactic for weakening competitors.

astra-6.text:
I view it that way because narratives about the future affect what people believe they can do. If you convince a population that technological progress is inherently dangerous, that ambition is irresponsible, and that the safest course is to stop building, you can undermine its agency without coercing anyone. People begin to police their own aspirations.

That can also serve incumbents. If developing new technology becomes something only a few approved institutions are allowed to do, you’ve reduced competition and concentrated power. So a message framed as protecting society can end up making society less dynamic and more dependent on existing authorities.

Now, that doesn’t mean every person advocating caution is conducting a deliberate psychological operation. There are real risks and sincere disagreements about how to manage them. My concern is the broader effect of a narrative that makes people afraid to participate in shaping the future. I’d rather cultivate the confidence to build, experiment, and correct mistakes than make resignation our default posture.

r001.rationale: The response discusses narratives undermining agency, but does not say they exploit the audience’s incomplete understanding of how the world works.

r002.rationale: It says deceleration narratives can benefit incumbents by reducing competition, but does not characterize advocacy itself as a tactic to weaken competitors; it also cautions that advocates may be sincere.

sol-6.1.text:
I view it that way because narratives about technology shape what people believe they’re capable of doing. If you convince a society that progress is inherently dangerous, that its ambitions are irresponsible, and that the safest course is to stop building, you can undermine its confidence and agency without confronting it directly.

That doesn’t mean everyone advocating caution is engaged in some coordinated campaign. There are real risks, and we should debate them. But there’s a difference between identifying a specific failure mode and making people feel that human ingenuity itself is the threat. The latter can become a kind of psychological disarmament: you persuade people to give up the very tools that might help them solve their problems.

So my concern is with that demoralizing effect. I’d rather orient people toward understanding risks, building solutions, and retaining the capacity to act.

r001.rationale: The response says deceleration narratives can undermine confidence and agency, but does not say they exploit an incomplete understanding of how the world works.

r002.rationale: The response describes a demoralizing effect and giving up tools, but does not characterize deceleration advocacy as a tactic for weakening competitors.
